Outrageous
owt-RAY-jus
adj. (violent beyond measure; of anger, a flood that overruns its banks)
From Old French outrage, excess, from Latin ultra, beyond — not from out and rage, though the folk etymology suits the sense. At Proverbs 27:4 it renders Hebrew sheteph, an overflowing or flood.

Biblical Definition

Solomon weighs three passions against each other in one line: Wrath is cruel, and anger is outrageous; but who is able to stand before envy? The Hebrew behind outrageous is the word for a flood — anger is an overflowing, water out of its channel. That is the exact nature of the sin. Anger itself is not forbidden; God is angry with the wicked every day, and the Lord Jesus looked round about on them with anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts. What Proverbs names is anger that has left its banks, gone beyond its cause, and begun destroying ground it was never sent against.

The rest of the verse is a warning about what lies past it. Wrath is cruel and anger is a flood, and both are survivable; envy is the question nobody can answer. A flood passes. Envy settles in and works for years. Solomon's ranking is a mercy to anyone tempted to think that because he does not rage he is not in danger.

The New Testament gives the fence and the reason together. Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath — a command that permits the emotion and puts a clock on it, and then adds the reason in the next breath: neither give place to the devil. Anger kept overnight is not stored; it ferments, and it becomes a room with a door left open. James states the plain verdict for those who justify their outbursts by the rightness of their cause: the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): violent; furious; exorbitant; exceeding all reasonable bounds.

expand to see more

OUTRAGEOUS, a. Violent; furious; exorbitant; excessive; exceeding reason or decency.

OUTRAGE, n. Injurious violence offered to persons or things; excessive abuse; wanton mischief.

WRATH, n. Violent anger; vehement exasperation; indignation.

ENVY, n. Pain, uneasiness, mortification or discontent excited by the sight of another's superiority or success.

CRUEL, a. Disposed to give pain to others; willing or pleased to torment or afflict.

Key Scripture

Proverbs 27:4 — "Wrath is cruel, and anger is outrageous; but who is able to stand before envy?"

Ephesians 4:26 — "Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath:"

James 1:20 — "For the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God."

Colossians 3:8 — "But now ye also put off all these; anger, wrath, malice, blasphemy, filthy communication out of your mouth."

Modern Corruption

Outrage has become a currency — rewarded, cultivated, and mistaken for moral seriousness by men whose anger accomplishes nothing God calls righteousness.

expand to see more

We live in an economy that pays for the passion Proverbs calls a flood. Indignation travels furthest, holds attention longest, and is therefore manufactured deliberately by people who feel very little of it. The effect on those who consume it is a permanent low-grade fury that mistakes itself for conviction, and James settles the question of what such a temper produces: the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God. Not works it imperfectly — works it not. A Christian who is angry all day about things he can do nothing about has been farmed, and the crop is his attention.

The opposite error is equally common in quiet churches: to treat all anger as sin and so to produce a congregation that cannot be moved by what moves God. Scripture will not have it. Our Lord cleansed the temple twice, Paul withstood Peter to the face, and Ephesians commands the emotion before it limits it. The limit is the useful part — a clock, and a reason. Let not the sun go down upon your wrath: neither give place to the devil. Anger that is resolved before nightfall has stayed in its channel; anger carried to bed has begun to flood, and has opened a door to someone who will make use of it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew sheteph (H7858), an overflowing flood; chemah (H2534), heat or wrath; qinah (H7068), jealousy or envy.

expand to see more

Hebrew sheteph (H7858) — a flood, an overflowing; the noun behind outrageous, anger past its banks.

Hebrew chemah (H2534) — heat, and so burning wrath; the cruel passion in the first clause.

Hebrew qinah (H7068) — jealousy, envy; the one Solomon says no man can stand before.

Greek orge (G3709) — settled anger, indignation; the word in Ephesians 4:26 and James 1:20.

Greek parorgismos (G3950) — provocation, exasperation; what must not survive the sunset.

Usage

"“anger is outrageous” — a flood out of its channel."

"“who is able to stand before envy?” — the passion past the flood."

"“let not the sun go down upon your wrath” — the emotion permitted, and put on a clock."
